title: Size it for the busiest minute

beats.say: Your platform handles an ordinary Tuesday. Will it survive launch day?

Every layer of a data foundation is sized for its peak, not its average. A product launch or a sale can bring four times the normal traffic for an hour, and the smallest layer decides whether the whole system holds.
Write the numbers down: events a second at peak, bytes per event, database writes, storage a year and queries an hour. Then size each layer from them.
If the arithmetic is written down, anyone can check that the design follows from it.

check.q: Which load should each layer of the foundation be sized for?
opts: The peak, such as launch day's traffic
The average over a normal working week
Whatever the vendor's default size offers
check.why: The smallest layer at peak decides whether the whole system holds.

work: Write your platform's average and peak events a second.
Name the layer that would fail first at four times the load.

title: From events to partitions

beats.say: One hundred thousand events a second at one kilobyte each. How many Kafka partitions?

Multiply events by size: one hundred megabytes a second. Divide by what one partition and one consumer task handle, say four megabytes a second: twenty-five. Add one and a half times headroom and round up: thirty-eight partitions.
Then size the rest the same way: stream tasks to match the partitions, database replicas for peak reads, and warehouse clusters for peak queries.
Always round up. A plan that rounds down is short of capacity at exactly the wrong moment.

check.q: Peak is 100 MB a second, a partition handles 4 MB a second, headroom 1.5. How many partitions?
opts: 38 partitions
25 partitions
150 partitions

work: Compute the partitions your busiest topic needs at peak.
Compare it with what the topic has today.

title: Price it per year and per unit

beats.say: The design holds at peak. What does it cost?
Add compute, storage, data transfer, licences and the people who run it, per year. People are often the largest line, and they are the one most often left out.
Then give unit costs that leaders can follow month by month: cost per terabyte scanned, per data product per month, per million events. A total alone hides whether you are getting more efficient.
Count the people. A cheap engine nobody can run is not cheap.

check.q: Which cost line is most often left out of a platform estimate?
opts: The people needed to run and support it
The compute used by the batch jobs each night
The storage for the raw data landing zone
check.why: People are often the largest line and the one most often forgotten.

work: Add the people cost to your platform's yearly estimate.
Pick one unit cost to report every month.

title: Three years, not one

beats.say: Option A is cheaper this year. Is it the right choice?

Foundations last for years and data keeps growing. Compare options over three years, with growth and with the people to run each. A managed warehouse may win in year one; an open lakehouse may win by year three, or the other way round.
In the review, show both totals, the assumptions behind them, and what would change your choice: faster growth, a smaller team, or a price change.
A decision with its numbers and its limits is one a CFO can approve.

check.q: How should a blueprint compare a warehouse with a lakehouse?
opts: Total cost over three years, with growth and people
This year's compute bill only, as finance asks
The price per credit shown on the vendors' pages
check.why: Growth and people often reverse the year-one choice.

work: Compare two options for your most expensive layer over three years.
Write one sentence on what would change your choice.

title: What a foundation blueprint is

beats.say: The CTO asks: what should our data platform be for the next three years?

A data foundation blueprint answers that in one document: the business and its numbers, principles, the architecture layer by layer, owners, the platform, governance, service levels, cost, a roadmap and risks.
Each decision in it names the alternative you rejected and why. That is what lets others trust it and change it later.
It sets one direction that every team can follow, instead of each team solving the same problems again.

check.q: What must every decision in a blueprint include?
opts: The alternative rejected and the reason why
The name of the engineer who first suggested it
A link to the vendor's marketing page for it
check.why: Alternatives and reasons let others trust and revise the decision.

work: List the ten parts for your company's platform.
Mark the two parts you know least about.

title: Why a blueprint beats the alternatives

beats.say: Why not just let each team choose, or rebuild everything at once?

With no plan, teams keep solving the same problems separately: many copies, unclear owners and surprise costs. A big-bang rebuild takes years and often never ships. A staged roadmap with dual runs delivers value every quarter and can stop safely.
And do not copy another company's architecture. Follow this company's numbers, constraints and skills.
A blueprint is a plan for this company, delivered in steps.

check.q: Why is a staged roadmap safer than a big-bang rebuild?
opts: It delivers value each quarter and can stop safely
It needs no reconciliation between old and new
It lets every team pick its own tools again
check.why: Each stage ships value and leaves the company in a working state.

work: Name one problem two of your teams solved separately.
Write the first stage of a staged plan for it.

title: When a blueprint is too much

beats.say: A startup with one data engineer and one database. Does it need a blueprint?

A small company needs a page of principles: open formats, change data capture instead of dumps, and cost tags from day one. A full three-year blueprint pays off when several teams, real cost and regulation are involved.

show.title: When to write the full one

beats.say: The common failure is the opposite: a long document nobody reads, a tool shopping list, or a plan without numbers.
Write as much plan as the company needs, and no more.

check.q: When does a full three-year blueprint pay off?
opts: When several teams, real cost and regulation are involved
As soon as the company hires its first data engineer
Only after every current system has been replaced
check.why: Below that, a page of principles is enough.

work: Decide whether your company needs a page or a full blueprint.
Write the page of principles either way.

title: Who writes it and who approves it

beats.say: Who owns the data foundation blueprint?

A staff or principal engineer writes it with the platform lead, domain leads, security and finance. The head of data or the CTO approves it. Writing it with the people who must follow it is how it gets followed.
It is funded as a programme with quarterly outcomes, and revised every half year with a dated change log.
Ownership is a name, a budget and a review date.

check.q: Who should review drafts of the blueprint?
opts: Domain leads, the platform team, security and finance
Only the architect who is writing it, to keep it fast
The vendors whose products the blueprint chooses
check.why: The people who must follow it shape it, so it gets followed.

work: List who would review your blueprint.
Set a date for its first half-year review.

title: The first 90 days

beats.say: Interview question: what do you do in the first 90 days of a foundation programme?
Build what everything else depends on: the catalog and its owners, cost tags with a first showback report, contracts and change data capture on the two busiest sources, and the first golden path.
Then ship one visible win for a real consumer, such as finance's daily revenue from one certified data product, faster and more reliable than before. And say what you are not doing yet.

chip.text: Say what you are not doing

beats.say: Foundations earn trust slowly. One early win earns the time to build them.

check.q: What belongs alongside the foundations in the first 90 days?
opts: One visible win for a real consumer
A full migration of every existing table
An evaluation of every vendor on the market
check.why: A win shows value early and buys time for the foundations.

work: Pick the visible win for your first 90 days.
Write what you will deliberately not do yet.

title: Migrating without stopping the business

beats.say: The old warehouse runs month-end close. How do you move off it?

Use the strangler pattern, domain by domain. Move one domain's sources through change data capture into the new tables, dual-run old and new, and reconcile them daily by key and by totals until they match.
Move consumers in groups with a rollback path. Keep the old system read-only through a full month-end close, then retire it on an announced date.
Numbers that match before cutover are what make a migration boring, and boring is the goal.

check.q: When is it safe to retire the old system?
opts: After the new one runs clean through a full month-end close
As soon as the new tables have been created and loaded
When the first consumer group has moved across to it
check.why: A full reporting cycle with matching numbers proves the new system.

work: Choose the first domain to migrate and say why.
Write the reconciliation checks you would run daily.

title: Risks and how a blueprint fails

beats.say: What could go wrong with your blueprint?

People, adoption, cost, migration, vendors and regulation. Too few engineers in domains, teams keeping old ways, spend outrunning value, numbers that do not match, a price change, a new residency rule.
Give each risk an owner, a response and an early warning number: the share of teams on the golden path, cost per query, reconciliation gaps. Watch the numbers monthly.
A blueprint that names its own risks is one a review can trust.

check.q: What should each risk in the blueprint have?
opts: An owner, a response and an early warning number
A promise that it will not happen this year
A long paragraph explaining why it is unlikely
check.why: Owners and early warning numbers turn risks into things you can act on.

work: List the top three risks for your foundation.
Give each one an early warning number.

title: Defending it in ten minutes

beats.say: Final round: present your data foundation in ten minutes.
One minute on the problem in numbers, one on principles, three on the architecture with a rejected alternative per layer, two on owners and governance, two on cost and the plan, one on risks.

Expect follow-ups: what breaks at ten times the load, what you cut with half the budget, how a region outage is handled. Answer with numbers and trade-offs, and say I don't know, here is how I would find out, when that is true.
Rehearse it out loud. The simulator's foundation challenge is your launch-day proof.

check.q: How long should the architecture take in a ten-minute blueprint review?
opts: About three minutes, with a rejected alternative per layer
All ten minutes, since the architecture is the design
Under a minute, so most time goes to the roadmap
check.why: The architecture gets the most time, but the problem, cost, plan and risks need theirs.

work: Time yourself presenting your blueprint out loud.
Answer the half-budget follow-up in two minutes.
